title: Model-Uncertainty-Aware Digital Twins for Non-Markovian Quantum Repeater Memories
abstract: Quantum-repeater controllers need reliable estimates of stored entanglement as adjacent links are generated. Fixed exponential lifetimes miss non-Markovian revivals, while complex surrogates are unnecessary when the microscopic family is known. We present QMemTwin, a physics-constrained digital twin that accounts for model uncertainty. It calibrates a bank of contractive passive state-space models, combines their amplitudes with finite-sample-corrected Akaike weights, and abstains when temporal-holdout data indicate unsupported dynamics. Passivity guarantees a completely positive, trace-preserving amplitude-damping channel for each candidate and their convex amplitude average. We evaluate [N cases] synthetic memories: [N supported] supported passive time-invariant cases and [N structural] nonstationary structural-shift cases. In the matched one-pseudomode regime, the correctly specified one-pseudomode fit performs best. Across [N unknown] supported cases with uncertain families, QMemTwin reduces population RMSE by [population reduction]% and Bell-fidelity RMSE by [Bell reduction]% relative to the two-pseudomode model; both paired effects remain significant after Holm correction. The flexible passive model has a slightly lower mean error for unknown families but is statistically indistinguishable from QMemTwin and loses accuracy in the matched regime. The temporal-holdout gate detects [detection]% of structural shifts, with [false alarm]% false alarms on supported families and AUROC [AUC]. In 2-, 4-, and 8-link repeater chains, the mixed cohort shows no significant 8-link goodput gain. A predeclared high-backflow stress cohort yields an 8-link goodput gain of [goodput gain]% over the two-pseudomode model, with paired p = [p value]. These results favor using a known family when available, accounting for model uncertainty otherwise and abstaining on unsupported dynamics.
summary: This paper introduces QMemTwin, a model-uncertainty-aware digital twin designed to estimate the evolution of entanglement in quantum repeater memories. It combines multiple candidate passive state-space models using weighted averaging and incorporates a safety gate to detect when the true dynamics fall outside the modeled family. The results demonstrate superior accuracy and robustness compared to simpler models, particularly in complex, non-Markovian network scenarios.
main_problem: Quantum-repeater controllers require reliable estimates of stored entanglement evolution, especially when the underlying memory dynamics are non-Markovian and subject to model uncertainty.
main_result: The proposed QMemTwin significantly reduces estimation errors (RMSE) compared to standard methods in supported memory regimes and provides a crucial safety mechanism (temporal-holdout gate) to abstain when dynamics are unsupported.
method: The authors developed QMemTwin, a digital twin that calibrates a bank of contractive passive state-space models and combines their predictions using finite-sample-corrected Akaike weights.
model_or_system: The system models quantum memories storing entangled Bell pairs, whose evolution is governed by non-Markovian dynamics. The methodology relies on characterizing the evolution using passive, contractive state-space models.
key_observables: Population RMSE, Bell-fidelity RMSE, qualified goodput (pairs/slot), and the detection rate of structural shifts.
important_parameters: The analysis covers various memory regimes, including single-pole, multi-pole, and coupled cases, and evaluates performance across 2-, 4-, and 8-link repeater chains.
main_assumptions: The method assumes the existence of a finite bank of candidate passive models and uses a temporal-holdout gate to manage model uncertainty and detect structural mismatches.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the QMemTwin workflow, comparing performance metrics (RMSE, goodput) across different memory families, and showing the efficacy of the adequacy gate in detecting structural shifts.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the QMemTwin methodology (calibration, weighting, gate), presents quantitative comparisons against existing controllers (2PM), and concludes with performance analysis in multi-hop quantum network simulations.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the practical challenges of quantum networking by providing a statistically rigorous and physically constrained tool to estimate quantum channel parameters under uncertainty, which is vital for scaling quantum communication.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. QMemTwin workflow and evaluation regimes. Sparse quadrature/population measurements calibrate passive candidates. AICc weights adapt complexity, a temporal-holdout gate determines model support, and only supported physical trajectories are exposed as network-facing fidelity, concurrence, uncertainty, and service windows. The higher-order family tests capacity mismatch; the nonstationary family is the structural-shift test.

Fig. 2. Representative trajectories for all six families. Sparse points end at Tobs = 6; shading denotes forecasting. The final row is structurally nonstationary and is used to test the adequacy gate, not to claim universal extrapolation. Negative exact time-local rates identify information-backflow intervals.

Fig. 3. Prediction and adaptive-complexity audit: supported-family errors, paired 95% intervals, AICc weights, sequential forecast error, and raw/projected TTM. Detailed six-panel source figures remain in the artifact.
Fig. 4. Adequacy, robustness, and uncertainty: support-score separation, structural-shift ROC/confusion, observation/noise sensitivity, bootstrap trajectory, and empirical coverage.

Figure 5 reports calibration cost versus accuracy. TTM- RAW is fast but exhibits catastrophic extrapolation in 2 of 40 supported cases: its mean population RMSE is 135.945, median 0.02479, and maximum 5329.0. The radial projection removes channel-domain violations and reduces mean error to 0.06742, but it is a post-hoc feasibility repair, not a guarantee that the recovered memory kernel is correct. Matrix pencil is also fast and competitive in several multi- exponential cases, but its pole truncation and stability projection degrade continuum/coupled cases.
